column1: In Cubase, what dBFS range should you target for input peaks when tracking audio, and why?
column2: -12 to -18 dBFS. Digital clipping hard-slices the waveform instantly at 0 dBFS (unlike musical analog saturation), so you track lower and use 24-bit headroom instead of chasing 0 dB.

column1: Why does digital clipping differ fundamentally from analog saturation?
column2: Analog tape/tube circuits round off peaks musically; digital clipping hard-slices the waveform the instant it exceeds 0 dBFS, producing harsh, unfixable distortion.

column1: What is the approximate dynamic range difference between 16-bit and 24-bit recording in Cubase?
column2: 16-bit gives ~96 dB of dynamic range; 24-bit gives ~144 dB, allowing safer recording levels without audible noise-floor penalty.

column1: What three pieces of data does a single MIDI note actually record in Cubase?
column2: Pitch (0–127, Middle C=60), velocity (0–127), and timing (Note On/Off messages measured in PPQ, typically 480 or 960 ticks/beat) — never the actual sound.

column1: In Cubase, what causes 'laggy keyboard' feel during MIDI tracking, and what's the fix?
column2: Large audio buffer size (ASIO), not MIDI transmission speed. Fix: drop buffer to ~128 samples (≈3ms at 44.1kHz) while tracking, then raise to 512–1024 for mixing.

column1: Why is changing tempo after recording MIDI safe, but changing tempo after recording audio is not?
column2: MIDI is tick-based (PPQ) and rescales automatically with tempo changes; audio is sample-based and requires time-stretching to match a new tempo, which is not free/lossless.

column1: What is the fixed internal signal order in a Cubase MixConsole channel strip?
column2: Input Gain → Pre-fader Inserts → EQ → Post-fader Inserts → Fader → Sends → Panner → Output.

column1: Can Cubase's internal 32/64-bit float engine actually 'clip' internally? Why do plugins still distort when driven hot?
column2: No, floating point summing has huge headroom and doesn't hard-clip internally. However, individual plugins (especially analog-modeled ones) have their own designed headroom and will saturate/distort character-fully if driven too hot, regardless of the engine's float math.

column1: What routing structure does Cubase explicitly prevent between channels?
column2: True feedback loops/cycles — you cannot send Channel A to Channel B and also route B back as a direct input to A; Cubase blocks this in the routing matrix.

column1: In Cubase automation, why does a Linear volume ramp often sound wrong compared to a Spline/Smooth curve?
column2: Linear ramps change value at a constant rate, but human hearing perceives loudness logarithmically, so a linear dB fade sounds like it changes faster near the end. Spline/Smooth eases in/out for a more natural, 'played' feel.

column1: What automation curve type should be used for mute automation or preset/program changes in Cubase, and why?
column2: Jump (step) curves — they hold a value until the next point then jump instantly, matching the discrete on/off nature of mutes and preset changes.

column1: How does ASIO Guard 2 let Cubase achieve both low tracking latency and CPU stability during mixing?
column2: It splits the engine into two lanes: a low-latency lane (small buffer, e.g. 32-128 samples) for armed/live-monitored tracks, and a high-latency pre-fetch lane (1024-8192 samples) for all other playback tracks, letting the CPU pre-render non-live material ahead of the playhead.
